chapters.name: Signs, Signals, and Pavement Markings
chapters.summary: What traffic lights, flashing signals, sign shapes and colors, and lane lines tell you to do. Questions here show a light, a sign, or a painted line and ask what you must do next; several use pictures of warning and regulatory signs such as Wrong Way, Slippery When Wet, Merge, Lane Ends, and Keep Right.
keyPoints: Red, steady or flashing, always means a full stop first. Flashing yellow never requires a stop, only a slower speed and extra care.
Dark or broken signal: every direction stops first, then drivers take turns.
Red arrow: no turn in that direction, even after a full stop. Steady red circle: a right turn after a full stop is allowed unless a sign says no.

Center lines: two solid yellow = no passing either way; broken yellow on your side = you may pass when it is clear; solid and broken yellow on each side of a lane = two-way left-turn lane, never for passing.
Count the sides: 8 = STOP, 5 = school zone or crossing. Downward triangle = YIELD, diamond = hazard ahead, round yellow with RR = railroad ahead, orange = work zone.

pitfalls.trap: A flashing yellow light means you must come to a full stop before going on.
pitfalls.fact: Only a red light, steady or flashing, requires a full stop. A flashing yellow is a warning: slow down and go through with extra care. Both lights blink, which is why people swap them, but only the flashing red acts like a stop sign.

pitfalls.trap: After a full stop at a red arrow, you may turn when the way is clear, the same as at a red circle.
pitfalls.fact: California allows a right turn after a full stop on a steady red circle unless a sign forbids it, but you may not turn on a red arrow at all. Wait until the arrow goes off or a green light or green arrow appears.

pitfalls.trap: The center lane with solid and broken yellow lines on both sides can be used to pass slow cars.
pitfalls.fact: That lane is a two-way center left-turn lane shared by both directions. Use it only to start or finish a left turn or a legal U-turn, never to pass or as a travel lane, because a driver from the other side may be turning in it.

chapters.name: Right of Way and Turns
chapters.summary: Who goes first at intersections, four-way stops, roundabouts, crosswalks, and when turning. Questions here describe one situation, such as two cars arriving together, pulling out of a driveway, reaching the end of a T-intersection, meeting on a steep mountain road, or hearing a siren mid-intersection, and ask who must yield or what to do.
keyPoints: Four-way stop: first to stop, first to go. Tie at a four-way stop or at an intersection with no signs or signals: the car on the left waits for the car on the right.
Roundabout: go counterclockwise, enter by turning right, and wait for a gap; cars already circling go first.
Every crosswalk counts, painted or unmarked at a corner. For a person with a white cane or guide dog, stop and do not honk.
Joining a road means yielding: from a driveway, from the end of a T-intersection, or from a freeway on-ramp, traffic already on the road goes first.
Turn signal: the last 100 feet before the turn. A left turn from a two-way street ends in the left lane nearest the center line of the new street.

pitfalls.trap: When two cars reach a four-way stop together, the car on the right yields to the car on the left.
pitfalls.fact: It is the reverse: the driver on the left yields, so the car on the right goes first. Vehicle size never decides who goes, and the same rule applies at an intersection with no signs or signals.

pitfalls.trap: If you hear a siren while you are already in an intersection, stop where you are.
pitfalls.fact: Never stop inside an intersection for an emergency vehicle, because you can block its path. Keep going through, then pull to the right as soon as it is safe and stop until it passes.

pitfalls.trap: On a narrow, steep road where two cars cannot pass, the driver going uphill should back down.
pitfalls.fact: The driver facing downhill backs up until the uphill car can get by. Many people guess the opposite, but the downhill driver has more control when backing up the hill.

chapters.name: Speed, Lanes, and Parking
chapters.summary: The Basic Speed Law, special speed limits, lane use, passing, and parking rules including curb colors. Most questions here ask for one exact number (mph, feet, or inches) or which way to turn your wheels on a hill, and the wrong choices are other numbers from the same short list, so learn the numbers together.
keyPoints: The posted limit is a ceiling, not a target. In fog, rain, or heavy traffic, even a speed under the limit can break the Basic Speed Law.

15 mph: alleys, and within 100 feet of a blind intersection or a railroad crossing where you cannot see 400 feet down the tracks both ways. 25 mph: residential districts, and within 500 feet of a school while children are outside or crossing.
55 mph on a two-lane undivided highway; 65 mph on most other highways, unless signs say otherwise.
Curbs: red = no stopping; yellow = stop only to load or unload passengers or freight; white = passenger or mail pickup only; green = time-limited parking; blue = disabled placard or plate only.
Parking distances: wheels within 18 inches of the curb, and at least 15 feet from a fire hydrant.
Hills with a curb: downhill, front wheels toward the curb; uphill, wheels away from it so the tire rolls back against the curb. Set the parking brake either way.
Right turn next to a bike lane: enter the bike lane within 200 feet of the corner after checking for riders, and start signaling at least 100 feet before the turn.

pitfalls.trap: As long as you are at or under the posted speed limit, you are obeying the speed law.
pitfalls.fact: California's Basic Speed Law says you may never drive faster than is safe for current conditions. In fog, heavy rain, or dense traffic the posted limit can be too fast, and matching the speed of the cars around you is not a defense.

pitfalls.trap: When parking uphill against a curb, you turn the front wheels toward the curb, the same as downhill.
pitfalls.fact: The two are opposites. Downhill: turn the wheels toward the curb. Uphill: turn them away from the curb and let the car roll back a few inches until the tire rests against it. Either way, the curb keeps the car from rolling into traffic.

pitfalls.trap: Before a right turn, you must stay out of the bike lane and turn from the lane to its left.
pitfalls.fact: In California you move into the bike lane within 200 feet of the corner, after signaling and checking for bicyclists, and turn from there. Turning across the bike lane from the next lane can hit a rider going straight.

chapters.name: Safe Driving and Sharing the Road
chapters.summary: Following distance, scanning, night and bad-weather driving, skids, and sharing the road with bicycles, motorcycles, trucks, and emergency vehicles. Questions here also cover California headlight rules, hydroplaning, railroad tracks, school buses with flashing red lights, and the Move Over law for vehicles stopped with flashing lights.
keyPoints: Following distance is counted in seconds, not car lengths: 3 seconds at minimum, more on wet roads or in fog.
Passing a bicycle: 3 feet of space at minimum; if the road is too narrow for that, slow down and wait.
Siren and red lights: pull to the right edge and stop. Vehicle stopped with flashing amber lights, such as a tow truck on the shoulder: move over a lane if safe, otherwise slow down.

Headlights on from 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise, and any time the wipers run continuously. Dim high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming car and 300 feet of a car you follow. Fog: low beams.
Skid: ease off the gas, do not slam the brakes, steer where you want to go. Hydroplaning: ease off the gas and keep the wheel straight.
Flashing red lights on a school bus: stay stopped until they go off, unless the bus is on the other side of a divided highway or a multilane highway (two or more lanes each way).

pitfalls.trap: You may pass a stopped school bus once the children are aboard, even if its red lights are still flashing.
pitfalls.fact: You must stay stopped as long as the red lights are flashing, not just until you think the children are on board. The exception is a bus on the other side of a divided highway or a multilane highway (two or more lanes in each direction), where you keep driving carefully.

pitfalls.trap: High beams help you see farther in fog.
pitfalls.fact: In fog, high beams bounce back off the fog and create glare, so you see less. Use low beams, slow down, and leave more following distance; if the fog is too thick, pull off the road safely.

pitfalls.trap: Roads are most slippery after it has rained steadily for hours.
pitfalls.fact: The first rain after a dry period is the most slippery, because oil and dirt on the road mix with the water. After hours of steady rain, much of that oil has been washed away.

chapters.name: Alcohol, Phones, and Licensing Laws
chapters.summary: Blood alcohol limits, implied consent, cell phone rules, seat belts and child seats, collision reporting, and insurance. Questions here also cover legal medicine and DUI, open containers, child car seat rules by age and height, and the night and passenger limits on a provisional license.
keyPoints: BAC limits by driver: 0.08% at 21 and older, 0.04% in a vehicle that requires a commercial license, 0.01% under 21.
Phones: adults hands-free only; drivers under 18 may not use one at all, even hands-free.
SR-1 report to the DMV: within 10 days if anyone was hurt or killed or damage is over $1,000. Every driver must have proof of financial responsibility, such as insurance.
Refusing a breath or blood test after a lawful DUI arrest is not a free choice: under implied consent it can cost you your license.
An opened alcohol container goes in the trunk or another area where no one sits, never in the glove box or under a seat.
Child seats: under 2, rear-facing unless 40 pounds or 40 inches; under 8, a car seat or booster in the back seat unless the child is 4 feet 9 inches or taller.

Provisional license, first 12 months: no driving from 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. and no passengers under 20, unless a licensed parent or guardian, a licensed adult 25 or older, or a certified instructor rides along.

pitfalls.trap: Legal medicine, prescription or over-the-counter, cannot lead to a DUI arrest.
pitfalls.fact: It is illegal to drive when any drug affects your ability to drive safely, including prescription and over-the-counter medicine. A prescription does not make impaired driving legal, so read the label for warnings such as drowsiness.

pitfalls.trap: A 17-year-old may talk on the phone while driving as long as it is hands-free.
pitfalls.fact: Hands-free use is allowed only for adult drivers. A driver under 18 may not use a cell phone at all while driving, even hands-free, except to call for help in an emergency.

pitfalls.trap: Every collision, even a minor one with no injuries, must be reported to the DMV on an SR-1.
pitfalls.fact: An SR-1 is required within 10 days only when someone is injured or killed or property damage is over $1,000. A crash with about $800 of damage and no injuries does not need one.
